name: Western Diamondback Rattlesnake
habitat: Deserts, dry grassland, scrub, rocky hillsides and farmland; often around ranches, barns and wood piles
range: South-western USA: Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Arizona and the far south of California, Nevada and Arkansas; into Mexico
diet: Rodents, rabbits, ground squirrels and birds
active: At dusk and night in summer, by day in spring and autumn
ids: A heavy rattlesnake with a broad, triangular head and a rattle at the tip of the tail.
Grey, tan or pinkish diamonds with pale edges run down the back; the pattern looks dusty and faded.
The tail just before the rattle has bold black and white rings of about equal width (a "coon tail").
Two pale diagonal lines on each side of the face; the rear one runs to the corner of the mouth.
Many small scales on top of the head between the eyes, vertical pupils and a heat-sensing pit below each eye.

look.head: Broad and triangular, with two pale stripes on the face
look.body: Heavy, with keeled scales and a rattle

fact: The black-and-white "coon tail" is shared only with the Mojave and Red Diamond Rattlesnakes; on the Mojave the white rings are wider than the black ones.

name: Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnake
habitat: Longleaf pine and wiregrass, pine flatwoods, palmetto scrub, coastal dunes and barrier islands
range: South-eastern USA: Florida, south Georgia, the Carolina coastal plain, south Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana
active: By day in cool weather, at dusk and night in summer
ids: A very large, thick rattlesnake: the heaviest venomous snake in the Americas.
Dark brown diamonds outlined in cream or yellow along the back, on an olive or brown body.
The tail is brownish with dark rings, not black and white, ending in a large rattle.
Two pale diagonal lines on each side of the head frame a dark band through the eye.

look.colour: Olive to dark brown, with cream or yellow edging
look.head: Broad and triangular, with a dark band through the eye between two pale lines
look.body: Massive and heavy, with a rattle

fact: It depends on gopher tortoise burrows for shelter, and has vanished from much of its range as longleaf pine forests were cleared.

name: Timber Rattlesnake
habitat: Forested hills with rocky ridges and winter dens; in the south, swamps, canebrakes and river-bottom forests
range: Eastern USA, from New Hampshire and New York to north Florida, west to Minnesota, Kansas and east Texas; gone from much of the north-east and from Canada
diet: Mice, chipmunks, squirrels and other small mammals
active: By day and at night; waits beside fallen logs for prey
ids: Dark crossbands shaped like a V or a chevron, pointing towards the head, on a yellow, tan, grey or nearly black body.
The tail is plain, velvety black just before the rattle.
Southern "canebrake" snakes are pinkish-tan, with a rusty stripe along the spine and a dark line from the eye.
Broad head with vertical pupils, usually without the bold pale face stripes of western rattlesnakes.

look.colour: Yellow, tan, grey or almost black; canebrakes pinkish-tan
look.pattern: Wavy V-shaped dark crossbands; black tail
look.head: Broad and triangular, mostly plain

fact: Timber Rattlesnakes can live for over 30 years and return to the same rocky den every winter.

name: Western Rattlesnake
habitat: Grassland, chaparral, oak woodland, rocky hillsides and forest edges, from the coast up into the mountains
range: Western USA and Canada: California, Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Nevada, Utah and southern British Columbia, with relatives across the Great Basin
diet: Ground squirrels, mice, rats, lizards and birds
active: By day in spring and autumn, at dusk and night in hot weather
ids: Dark, blotchy diamonds or hexagons with pale borders on a brown, grey or olive body; towards the tail the blotches join into crossbands.
The tail rings are brown and pale, not crisp black and white, and often end in a wider dark ring before the rattle.
A pale stripe runs from behind the eye towards the corner of the mouth.
Triangular head, vertical pupils, heat-sensing pits and a rattle.

look.pattern: Pale-edged dark blotches that turn into bands on the tail
look.head: Broad and triangular, with a pale stripe behind the eye
look.body: Medium to heavy, with a rattle

fact: In California it is often confused with the harmless Gophersnake, which copies a rattlesnake by hissing and shaking its tail in dry leaves.

name: Prairie Rattlesnake
habitat: Short-grass prairie, sagebrush, badlands and rocky outcrops; often in prairie-dog towns
range: The Great Plains, from Alberta and Saskatchewan through Montana, the Dakotas, Wyoming, Nebraska, Colorado and Kansas to New Mexico and west Texas
diet: Prairie dogs, ground squirrels, mice and birds
active: By day in spring and autumn, at night in summer
ids: Greenish-brown, olive or tan with dark brown, pale-edged blotches that become crossbands near the tail.
Two pale lines on each side of the face; the rear one passes behind the corner of the mouth.
The tail has brown rings, not black-and-white ones, and ends in a rattle.
Broad triangular head with vertical pupils.

look.pattern: Rounded dark blotches with pale edges
look.head: Triangular, with two pale face lines

fact: In the northern prairies hundreds may share one winter den, then spread out over the grassland in spring.

name: Mojave Rattlesnake
habitat: Open desert flats and scrub with creosote and mesquite, and desert grassland
range: The Mojave and Chihuahuan Deserts: south-eastern California, southern Nevada and Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas; into Mexico
diet: Kangaroo rats, mice and other rodents, and lizards
active: Mostly at dusk and night
ids: Looks like a Western Diamondback but is often greenish, with crisper, well-defined diamonds.
On the tail the white rings are clearly wider than the black ones.
The pale stripe behind the eye passes above the corner of the mouth.
Two or three large scales between the eyes on top of the head (the Western Diamondback has many small ones).

look.pattern: Crisp pale-edged diamonds; white tail rings wider than the black
look.head: Triangular, with large scales between the eyes

fact: Many Mojave Rattlesnakes carry "Mojave toxin", which attacks the nerves, so a bite can be dangerous even when the wound looks mild.

name: Sidewinder
habitat: Sandy desert with dunes, creosote flats and washes
range: The Mojave and Sonoran Deserts: south-eastern California, southern Nevada, south-western Utah and western Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, kangaroo rats and pocket mice
active: Mostly at night; by day it buries itself in sand under bushes
ids: A small, pale rattlesnake with a raised, horn-like scale above each eye.
Moves by "sidewinding", throwing its body sideways and leaving a row of J-shaped tracks in the sand.
Cream, tan, pink or grey to match the sand, with faint darker blotches.
A rattle on the tail, and a triangular head with vertical pupils.

look.head: Triangular, with a horn over each eye
look.body: Short and stout, with a rattle

fact: Sidewinding lets it cross loose, hot sand with only two short parts of its body touching the ground at a time.

name: Southwestern Speckled Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky desert slopes, canyons and boulder fields
range: Southern California, southern Nevada, south-western Utah and western Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Mice, kangaroo rats, lizards and birds
active: By day in cool weather, at night in summer
ids: Its colour matches the local rock: cream, pink, orange, grey or almost black.
A grainy, "peppered" pattern of indistinct crossbands, as if sprinkled with dark specks.
Dark rings on the tail before the rattle.
Triangular head with vertical pupils; the scales look rough and sandpapery.

look.colour: Cream, pink, orange, grey or dark, like the rocks it lives on
look.head: Triangular

fact: Snakes on pink granite are pink, those on dark lava are nearly black: one of the best-camouflaged rattlesnakes.

name: Panamint Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky desert mountains, canyons and alluvial fans
range: The desert ranges of eastern California and southern Nevada, such as the Panamint and Inyo Mountains
active: By day in cool weather, at night in summer
ids: A pale, speckled rattlesnake of desert mountains, tan to grey with faint crossbands.
The bands are made of fine dark specks rather than solid colour.
Dark rings on the tail and a rattle.
fact: It was long treated as part of the Speckled Rattlesnake and was recognised as its own species in 2007.

name: Northern Black-tailed Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky canyons, oak and pine woodland and desert mountains
range: Arizona and western New Mexico; into Mexico
active: By day in cool weather, at dusk and night in summer
ids: Olive, yellow or greenish, with dark crossbands that have pale centres.
Many scales are a single colour, light or dark, which gives a patchwork look.
The tail is solid black, and the snout is usually dark too.
fact: It is famously calm for a rattlesnake and often rattles only as a last resort.

name: Eastern Black-tailed Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky slopes and canyons of the Chihuahuan Desert and its mountains
range: West Texas and southern New Mexico; into Mexico
active: By day in cool weather, at night in summer
ids: Grey to olive with dark crossbands, often edged with pale scales.
Solid black tail before the rattle.
Only told from the Northern Black-tailed Rattlesnake by where it lives.
fact: Its separation from the Northern Black-tailed Rattlesnake rests on DNA rather than looks.

name: Rock Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky slopes, canyons and talus in desert mountains
range: West Texas, southern New Mexico and south-eastern Arizona; into Mexico
active: By day
ids: A small rattlesnake with dark crossbands spaced widely along a pale grey, greenish or pinkish body.
Banded snakes have bold black bands; mottled snakes have bands made of dark specks.
A dark stripe from the eye to the corner of the mouth.
A small rattle and a rather small head.

look.colour: Pale grey, greenish, bluish or pinkish
look.head: Small, with a dark stripe behind the eye
look.body: Small and fairly slim for a rattlesnake

fact: Its colours tend to match the rocks: greenish in some ranges, pinkish or grey in others.

name: Tiger Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky canyons and slopes in the Sonoran Desert
range: Arizona; into Sonora, Mexico
active: Mostly at night
ids: Grey, pinkish or lavender, with many thin, wavy crossbands like tiger stripes.
A very small head for a rattlesnake, with a large rattle.
The bands become clearer and darker towards the tail.
fact: It produces only a little venom, but drop for drop it is among the most toxic of all rattlesnake venoms.

name: Ridge-nosed Rattlesnake
habitat: Pine-oak woodland and rocky canyons in high mountains
range: Sky-island mountains of south-eastern Arizona and south-western New Mexico; into Mexico
active: By day
ids: A small brown rattlesnake with a raised ridge along the edge of its snout.
Bold white stripes on the face.
Thin pale crossbars edged in dark brown along the back.

look.head: Small, with white face stripes and a ridged snout

fact: It is Arizona's state reptile.

name: Twin-spotted Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky slopes and talus in high pine-oak forest
range: The highest mountains of south-eastern Arizona; into Mexico
active: By day
ids: A small, slim grey rattlesnake with pairs of small dark spots side by side down the back.
Speckled with tiny dark flecks between the spots.
A tiny rattle.

look.pattern: Paired dark spots down the back
look.head: Small
look.body: Small and slim, with a tiny rattle

fact: In Arizona it lives only on a few mountain tops above about 2,000 m.

name: Red Diamond Rattlesnake
habitat: Coastal sage scrub, chaparral, rocky hillsides and desert foothills
range: Southern California; into Baja California
diet: Ground squirrels, rabbits and other mammals
active: By day in spring, at dusk and night in summer
ids: Brick-red, pinkish or tan, with pale-edged diamonds.
A black-and-white ringed tail before the rattle, like the Western Diamondback.
Large and heavy, with a broad triangular head.
fact: Despite its size it is usually mild-tempered, but its bite is dangerous like any large rattlesnake's.

name: Arizona Black Rattlesnake
habitat: Rocky canyons and mountain woodland
range: Central and eastern Arizona and western New Mexico
active: By day in cool weather, at night in summer
ids: Adults are dark grey to black, with pale crossbars or rings of light scales.
It can darken and lighten its colour within minutes.
Young snakes are grey-brown with dark blotches, like other Western Rattlesnakes.
fact: Mothers stay with their newborn young for days, and families have been seen sharing dens.

name: Pygmy Rattlesnake
habitat: Pine flatwoods, wet prairies, marshes and swamp edges
range: South-eastern USA: Florida to North Carolina, west to Oklahoma and east Texas
active: By day and at night
ids: A small, stout rattlesnake with a tiny rattle that buzzes like an insect.
Grey (reddish in the Carolinas) with rows of black blotches and often a rust or orange stripe down the spine.
Large plates on top of the head, unlike the small scales of most other rattlesnakes.

look.pattern: Rows of dark blotches with an orange spine stripe
look.head: Triangular, with large head plates
look.body: Small and stout, with a tiny rattle

fact: Its rattle is so small it can hardly be heard more than a metre away.

name: Eastern Massasauga
habitat: Wet prairies, fens, bogs and swamp edges; drier fields in summer
range: The Great Lakes region: southern Ontario, Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and New York
diet: Voles, mice, frogs and small snakes
active: By day in spring and autumn, at night in summer
ids: Grey or brownish-grey with large dark brown blotches down the back and smaller ones on the sides.
Nine large plates on top of the head and a small rattle.
A dark stripe through the eye, edged with white.

look.colour: Grey to grey-brown; some are all black
look.head: Triangular, with large head plates

fact: It is Ontario's only venomous snake, and is protected as threatened in both Canada and the USA.

name: Western Massasauga
habitat: Grassland, prairie and desert grassland, often near water
range: The Great Plains: Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Nebraska, Colorado, New Mexico and Missouri; into Mexico
active: By day in spring and autumn, at night in summer
ids: A small, pale grey or tan rattlesnake with rows of brown blotches.
Large plates on top of the head and a small rattle.
Told apart from the Eastern Massasauga mainly by where it lives.

look.head: Triangular, with large head plates
look.body: Small and stout, with a small rattle

fact: Unlike most rattlesnakes it often lives near water and eats many frogs.

name: Eastern Copperhead
habitat: Forests, rocky hillsides, woodland edges and suburbs with leaf litter, wood piles and old walls
range: Eastern USA, from Massachusetts and New York to north Florida, west to Illinois, Missouri and east Texas
diet: Mice, frogs, lizards and insects such as cicadas
active: By day in spring and autumn, at night in summer
ids: Copper, pinkish or tan, with dark hourglass-shaped crossbands: wide on the sides, narrow over the back.
A plain, unmarked coppery head with vertical pupils and a heat-sensing pit.
Young snakes have a bright yellow-green tail tip.
No rattle. Stout body with keeled scales.
fact: Copperheads bite more people in the eastern USA than any other snake, but their bites are very rarely fatal.

name: Broad-banded Copperhead
habitat: Woodland, rocky hills, river bottoms and suburbs
range: Texas, Oklahoma and southern Kansas
active: By day in spring and autumn, at night in summer
ids: Very broad reddish-brown crossbands that hardly narrow over the back, on a pale tan body.
A plain coppery head with vertical pupils.
Young have a yellow-green tail tip.
fact: The western copperheads were split from the Eastern Copperhead as their own species in 2015.

name: Northern Cottonmouth
habitat: Swamps, marshes, slow rivers, ponds, bayous and ditches
range: South-eastern and south-central USA: Virginia to Alabama, west to Texas and Oklahoma, and up the Mississippi to southern Illinois and Indiana
diet: Fish, frogs, snakes, small mammals and birds
active: By day and at night
ids: Heavy-bodied and dark: olive, brown or nearly black; adults often look plain, with only faint crossbands.
A broad, flat-topped head with a dark stripe through the eye (a "mask") and vertical pupils.
When threatened it gapes to show the white inside of its mouth.
It swims with its whole body floating high on the water.
Young are boldly banded like copperheads, with a yellow tail tip.

look.head: Broad and blocky, with a dark mask through the eye
look.body: Heavy, with a short, thick tail

fact: Most "water moccasins" reported by people are in fact harmless watersnakes, which are far more common.

name: Florida Cottonmouth
habitat: Swamps, marshes, lakes, canals and wet prairies
range: Florida and south Georgia
diet: Fish, frogs, snakes, birds and carrion
active: By day and at night
ids: A heavy, dark water snake: brown to black, with faint wide crossbands.
A bold dark mask through the eye, often edged by pale lines on the snout, and vertical pupils.
Gapes to show its cotton-white mouth when disturbed.

look.head: Broad, with a dark mask and pale facial lines

fact: It often stays put rather than fleeing, but it will bite only if stepped on or handled.

name: Harlequin Coral Snake
habitat: Pine flatwoods, sandhills, hardwood hammocks and gardens; hides in leaf litter and under logs
range: South-eastern USA: Florida, south Georgia, the Carolina coastal plain, south Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana
active: Mostly by day, at dawn and dusk
ids: Glossy rings of red, yellow and black around the body; the red rings touch the narrow yellow rings.
A blunt black snout, then a wide yellow band across the back of the head.
Slim, smooth and shiny, with a small head no wider than the neck.
The tail has only black and yellow rings.

look.head: Small and blunt, with a black snout

fact: In the USA "red touches yellow" marks a coral snake, but the rhyme fails elsewhere in the world, so never rely on it to handle a snake.

name: Texas Coral Snake
habitat: Woodland, thornscrub, rocky canyons and suburban gardens
range: Texas, Louisiana and southern Arkansas; into Mexico
active: By day, especially after rain
ids: Wide red and black rings separated by narrow yellow rings; red touches yellow.
The red rings are often flecked with black.
A black snout and a yellow band behind the head.

look.head: Small and blunt, with a black snout

fact: It looks almost exactly like the Harlequin Coral Snake; the two are told apart mainly by range.

name: Sonoran Coral Snake
habitat: Rocky desert, thornscrub and grassland, often hiding under stones
range: Arizona and south-western New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Thread snakes and other small snakes
active: At night and after summer rains
ids: A small coral snake with wide red and black rings separated by white or pale yellow rings.
A black head with a pale band behind it.
Red touches the pale rings.

look.colour: Red, black and white or pale yellow
look.head: Black, small and rounded

fact: When alarmed it makes a popping sound by pushing air out of its vent.
